newsitem.title: THAILAND: Thai economy set to weaken further - Salomon.
newsitem.headline: Thai economy set to weaken further - Salomon.

text.p: Salomon Brothers on Tuesday said the Thai economy was expected to weaken further and predicted a mounting bad debt cycle would cause earnings growth in the financial sector to slow.

"The firm expects margins to be negatively impacted by a number of factors, including a rise in non-performing loans, increased interest rate sensitivity and the results of Bank of Thailand funding restrictions," it said in a statement.
Salomon said Thailand's ailing property market accounted for a disproportionate percentage of most bank's non-performing loans.

"Property companies ... may not be able to service their loans to the banks. As the property slump continues, the main casue being the relentless increases in supply versus continual low levels of demand, we expect NPLs (non-performing loans) to increase further," Salomon said.
Salomon's Thai financial institutions analyst Donaldson Hartman said declining loan quality, slowing economic growth rates, and provisioning could cause Thai banks' earnings to slump.
"At worst with 25 percent of real estate loans becoming doubtful, the decline on net income before provisioning expenses will reach 39.1 percent, or 49.3 percent after provisioning," he said.
Andrew Freris Salomon's chief regional economist, said banks' earnings slowdown would be exaggerated by a further weakening of the economy.
"Most indicators point to a further weakening of the economy, though there are signs of it stabilising, with GDP growth declining to 7.5 percent in 1996," he said.

Salomon said slowing growth, reduced capital inflows and the likelihood of interest rates remaining at current levels would contribute to a continued fall in banks' loan growth and rising funding costs.
"This will add more pressure to the bank's net interest margins. We expect to see a drop in net interest margins in 1996 and 1997 which will further affect banks' income," Freris and Hartman said.

"Other signs of a bad debt cycle in Thailand include untimely and weak charge-off and provisioning policies, higher rates of bounced cheques, sharp increases in accrued interest and the Bank of Thailand's action to halt the calling of finance company loans," the statement said.
